subject: biology
title: Culturing microorganisms and aseptic technique
key_idea: Bacteria multiply by **binary fission**, and can be grown (cultured) on agar in a Petri dish. **Aseptic technique** keeps unwanted microorganisms out. A clear zone around an antibiotic disc shows where bacteria were killed, and its area is calculated with πr².

sections.heading: How bacteria grow and how to count them

blocks.text: Bacteria reproduce by simple cell division. This section covers the conditions they need and how to work out numbers.

items.meaning: One bacterial cell dividing to make two.
A population of microorganisms grown in the laboratory.
A jelly containing nutrients that bacteria grow on in a Petri dish.

items: Bacteria can divide as often as once every 20 minutes, if they have enough nutrients and a suitable temperature.
To keep a high rate of reproduction, add more sugar, amino acids and oxygen.
Also keep a suitable temperature, remove toxins and waste, maintain the pH, and stir the culture.

blocks.label: Number of bacteria
where: n is the number of divisions
n = time ÷ time for one division

items.text: One bacterium divides every 20 minutes. In 2 hours (120 minutes): n = 120 ÷ 20 = 6.

items: Dilute each sample, and count the bacteria using a microscope.
Find the mean number of bacteria. Example: (15 + 12 + 13 + 16) ÷ 4 = 14.
Scale up to 1 cm³. If each sample is 0.02 cm³, multiply the mean by 50.
Bacteria multiply by binary fission, as often as every 20 minutes in good conditions.
The number doubles with every division.
Take a mean of several samples, then scale up to estimate the number in 1 cm³.

blocks.text: Aseptic technique stops unwanted microorganisms getting into the culture and stops harmful bacteria escaping.

items.meaning: Methods that prevent contamination of a culture by unwanted microorganisms.
Kill all microorganisms on equipment or in agar, for example in an autoclave.
Put bacteria onto the agar, for example using an inoculating loop.

items.text: Sterilise the Petri dish and agar before use, for example in an autoclave. This kills unwanted microorganisms.
Melt the agar, pour it into the Petri dish, and let it cool and set.
Pass the inoculating loop through a Bunsen flame to sterilise it, then let it cool so the bacteria are not killed.
Collect a sample of bacteria with the loop and spread it over the agar. Lift the lid only a little.
Seal the lid with tape, but not all the way round. Some air must get in.
Incubate the dish upside down, at 25 °C in school.

items: Working near a Bunsen flame creates an upward air current. It stops microorganisms in the air falling onto the plate.
Disinfect the work surface, and keep the lid on for as short a time as possible when it is off.
Taping the lid stops microorganisms getting in or out. Leaving a gap lets oxygen in, so that harmful bacteria that do not need oxygen do not grow.
School cultures are kept at 25 °C, which prevents the growth of bacteria that are harmful to humans.
Scientists studying bacteria that infect humans may use 37 °C, which is body temperature, where those bacteria grow best.
Sterilise equipment and agar, flame the loop, and lift the lid only a little.
Aseptic technique prevents contamination.
School cultures are incubated at 25 °C so that harmful bacteria do not grow.

blocks.text: To test an antibiotic or antiseptic, a paper disc soaked in it is placed on a plate of bacteria. Where the bacteria are killed, a clear area forms.

items.meaning: The clear area around a disc where no bacteria are growing.
A disc soaked in water, with no antibiotic, to show the effect of no antibiotic.

items: A bigger zone of inhibition means the antibiotic killed more bacteria.
Measure the diameter or radius of the clear area. Radius = diameter ÷ 2.
Repeat the investigation and calculate a mean to improve it.
If bacteria are resistant to an antibiotic, none of them are killed and there is no clear zone.

blocks.label: Area of a zone of inhibition
where: r is the radius of the clear zone, in mm

items.text: The zone has a diameter of 9 mm, so the radius is 9 ÷ 2 = 4.5 mm.

items: A larger clear zone means the antibiotic is more effective.
Use the radius in πr². Halve the diameter first.
A control disc with no antibiotic shows the effect of the disc alone.

checks.q: Why is the inoculating loop passed through a flame, and then left to cool?
checks.a: To sterilise it and kill unwanted microorganisms. It cools so that it does not kill the bacteria being transferred.

worked_example.question: A student investigated the effect of antibiotics on the growth of bacteria. The student prepared an agar gel plate using standard laboratory equipment (Petri dish, agar, Bunsen burner, inoculating loop, disinfectant). Describe a method the student could use to prepare a sterile agar gel plate, and to grow an uncontaminated sample of bacteria on the agar gel plate.
answer_points: Preparation of the plate: melt the agar, pour it into the Petri dish, and allow it to cool and set.
Transfer of bacteria: spread the bacteria on the agar using an inoculating loop, or pour on a liquid culture.
Aseptic technique: disinfect the table or hands, sterilise the agar and Petri dish (autoclave or heating), pass the loop through a flame, work next to a Bunsen flame, and lift the lid only a little.
Growth: tape the lid on correctly, incubate the dish upside down at 25 °C.
worked_example.tip: Marks are by level. The top level needs the preparation of the plate, the transfer of bacteria, and sterile technique, in a logical order.

worked_example.question: A filter paper disc soaked in toothpaste mixed with saliva (disc A) was placed on an agar jelly plate of bacteria and kept at 37 °C for 24 hours. The diameter of the zone of inhibition around disc A is 9 mm. Calculate the area of this zone of inhibition using the equation πr². Use a value of 3.14 for π. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
worked_example.tip: Full marks for the correct answer without working. If the diameter is used by mistake, one or two marks can still be given.

worked_example.question: Farmers sometimes give farm animals antibiotics, even if the animals are not ill. Scientists tested to see if bacteria in samples from farm animals were killed by the antibiotics. Describe how you would use this equipment to test if bacteria are killed by an antibiotic. Equipment: Petri dish with bacteria growing on nutrient agar; laboratory incubator; filter paper discs; antibiotic.
answer_points: Soak the filter paper discs in the antibiotic.
Place the discs on the surface of the nutrient agar.
Put the dish in the incubator.
After a few days look to see if there is a clear area around the disc.
worked_example.tip: Any three score one mark each. Putting antibiotic straight onto the bacteria or Petri dish is ignored.
